facts.kid: Astrobee robots are three flying cubes on the space station called Honey, Queen and Bumble. Fans inside an Astrobee blow air out of little nozzles, so the Astrobee can float around. An Astrobee can grab a handrail with its arm to rest, and recharges at a docking station.

source.title: Astrobee - NASA

facts.kid: Buzz Aldrin was the lunar module pilot on Apollo 11. On July 20, 1969, Buzz Aldrin climbed down right after Neil Armstrong, becoming the second person to walk on the Moon. Three years earlier, on Gemini XII, Buzz Aldrin did a spacewalk outside the spacecraft.

source.title: Former Astronaut Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin - NASA

facts.kid: Chiaki Mukai is a doctor who became the first Japanese woman in space in 1994 on Space Shuttle Columbia. Chiaki Mukai flew again in 1998 with John Glenn. In space, Chiaki Mukai wrote the start of a short Japanese poem called a tanka about doing somersaults, and people on Earth were asked to finish it.

source.title: STS-65 - NASA

facts.kid: Guion Bluford, called Guy, was a U.S. Air Force fighter pilot and engineer. On August 30, 1983, Guion Bluford flew on Space Shuttle Challenger's STS-8 mission and became the first African American in space. Guion Bluford flew to space four times in total.

source.title: Celebrating Guy Bluford's Historic First Flight - NASA

facts.kid: Neil Armstrong was the commander of Apollo 11. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong steered the lunar module Eagle down to a flat area called the Sea of Tranquility and became the first person ever to step onto the Moon. Neil Armstrong called the landing spot Tranquility Base.

source.title: Neil A. Armstrong - NASA

facts.kid: Each astronaut breathes in a little less than 1 kilogram of oxygen every day, about 0.9 kg in NASA's newest planning numbers. Bigger, more active people use more; smaller people use less. A Moon base must make or store this oxygen for every crew member, every day.

source.title: Developing an Advanced Life Support System for the Flexible Path into Deep Space (Jones & Kliss, 2010)
source.publisher: NASA Technical Reports Server (Ames Research Center)

facts.kid: In April 1984, Rakesh Sharma, an Indian Air Force pilot, became the first Indian to go to space. Rakesh Sharma rode a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft to the Salyut 7 space station for about eight days. When India's Prime Minister asked how India looked from space, Rakesh Sharma answered 'Sare Jahan Se Accha', meaning the best in the world.

source.title: HSFC - Human Space Flight Centre: Astronaut Corner
source.publisher: Human Space Flight Centre, ISRO (Government of India)

facts.kid: Sunita Williams lived on the space station three times and was its commander twice. Sunita Williams spent 608 days in space and did nine spacewalks, more spacewalk time than any other woman. Sunita Williams flew up on Starliner in 2024, came home on a SpaceX Dragon in 2025, and retired from NASA in December 2025.

source.title: NASA Astronaut Suni Williams Retires - NASA

facts.kid: NASA plans that each astronaut drinks about 2 liters of water a day and uses about half a liter more to prepare food. Extra water is needed for sweat from exercise and for washing. At an early Moon base, one astronaut may use about 4.5 liters of water every day.

source.title: Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (NASA/TP-2015-218570/REV2)

facts.kid: Earth has two shields. Its magnetic field is like an invisible bubble that pushes most charged particles away. Then the thick air soaks up most of the particles that still get in. That is why we are safe on the ground, but astronauts far from Earth are not.

source.title: Real Martians: How to Protect Astronauts from Space Radiation on Mars

facts.kid: The Electrodynamic Dust Shield uses electricity, with no moving parts or brushes, to push Moon dust off a surface. In March 2025 it was tested on the Moon aboard Firefly's Blue Ghost lander and cleaned dust off glass and a radiator. Later it could help keep solar panels clean.

source.title: NASA's Dust Shield Successfully Repels Lunar Regolith on Moon

facts.kid: Electrolysis means sending electricity through water to break it into two gases: oxygen and hydrogen. The space station makes the air astronauts breathe this way. Most of water's weight is oxygen: 1 kg of water gives about 0.89 kg of oxygen and 0.11 kg of hydrogen.

source.title: Technology Assessment for Producing Propellant From Lunar Water
source.publisher: NASA Technical Reports Server (Johnson Space Center)

facts.kid: A small nuclear reactor makes heat by splitting atoms and turns that heat into electricity. It works day and night, even in dark craters. NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy are working on one called Lunar Reactor-1, aiming to have it ready to launch by 2030. None is on the Moon yet.

source.title: NASA, Department of Energy to Develop Lunar Surface Reactor by 2030

facts.kid: NASA's rules say space food should give each astronaut about 3,035 kilocalories a day on average. That is a planning target. NASA can also work out a personal number for each astronaut from their body size and how active they will be.

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-013: Food and Nutrition (Rev D)
source.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer

facts.kid: Oxygen slowly spoils food and makes it taste stale. So before sealing some space food pouches, NASA pulls out the air and fills them with nitrogen gas, which does not react with the food. This keeps food tasting better for longer.

source.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew Illness Due to an Inadequate Food System (Perchonok, Douglas, Cooper)
source.publisher: NASA Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center

facts.kid: Space food comes in single-serving pouches made of several thin layers stuck together. Many pouches have a layer of aluminum foil, which blocks oxygen and moisture so the food stays good longer. Some clear plastic pouches have no foil, so they get an extra foil wrapper.

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-013: Food and Nutrition (Rev D)
source.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer

facts.kid: Heat, damp air and oxygen all make stored food go bad faster. Space food is made to last a long time at room temperature, about one and a half years. A trip to Mars would need food that lasts five years, so NASA is still working on better packaging and storage.

source.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew Illness Due to an Inadequate Food System (Perchonok, Douglas, Cooper)
source.publisher: NASA Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center

facts.kid: Astronaut food comes in several kinds: heat-treated pouches, dried foods you add water to, snacks like nuts and cookies that are ready to eat, some fresh fruit, and drinks. The space station has a food warmer to heat pouches and a water dispenser for hot or room-temperature water.

source.title: NASA Facts: Space Food (FS-2006-11-029-JSC)

facts.kid: Dried space food needs water before you can eat it, and warming food needs electricity. On a spacecraft, water and power are limited, so NASA plans meals carefully. That is why meals in the game cost water and power.

source.title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-013: Food and Nutrition (Rev D)
source.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer

facts.kid: Rockets need two things to burn: a fuel and oxygen. Split Moon water and you get both! Hydrogen is the fuel and oxygen helps it burn. Chilled into liquids, they can fill a rocket's tanks, so rockets could refuel on the Moon instead of bringing all their propellant from Earth.

source.title: Technology Assessment for Producing Propellant From Lunar Water
source.publisher: NASA Technical Reports Server (Johnson Space Center)

facts.kid: Plants need water and nutrients at their roots. On the space station, NASA tested XROOTS, which grows plants without soil using nutrient-rich water (hydroponics) or a nutrient mist (aeroponics). Older space gardens like Veggie use small clay-filled pillows instead.

source.title: NASA's SpaceX Crew-5 Scientific Mission aboard the Space Station

facts.kid: ISRU stands for In-Situ Resource Utilization. In-situ means 'in place'. It means using what you find on the Moon, like ice and rocks, to make water, air and rocket fuel, instead of carrying everything from Earth. It is like camping and getting water from a stream instead of packing it all.

source.title: Overview: In-Situ Resource Utilization

facts.kid: One day-and-night on the Moon takes about 29.5 Earth days. At the Moon's middle, daytime lasts about 14 Earth days, then night lasts about 14 Earth days. Near the South Pole, some high crater rims get sunlight almost all the time, while some deep craters stay dark.

source.title: Lunar Daylight Exploration

facts.kid: Moon dust is sharp and sticky because it carries an electric charge, so it clings to things. If dust covers a solar panel, less sunlight reaches it and it makes less electricity. In one NASA lab test, a thin dust layer cut a solar cell's power by almost 40 percent.

source.title: Lunar Dust Considerations for Vertical Solar Arrays, Volume 1 (NASA/TM-20240003496)

facts.kid: Near the Moon's South Pole, some crater floors never see the Sun. They can be colder than -198 degrees Celsius. Water molecules that hop across the Moon and land there freeze and get stuck, like food in a freezer that never turns off. That is why scientists think ice is hiding there.

source.title: NASA's LRO: Lunar Ice Deposits are Widespread

facts.kid: A Moon rover can't plug a cable into Earth. Instead it sends its data as radio waves. Giant dish antennas on Earth, in NASA's Deep Space Network and Near Space Network, catch those signals. NASA is building new dishes called LEGS just for Moon missions.

source.title: VIPER Rover and Instruments

facts.kid: Earth is wrapped in thick air and a strong magnetic bubble. The Moon has almost no air (just a super-thin layer of gas) and only very weak magnetism. Neither one protects you, so space radiation reaches the Moon’s surface almost freely.

source.title: Earth’s Moon: Facts

facts.kid: In the game, some places protect you better than others. That idea is real: a spacesuit is thin and gives very little radiation protection, while a storm shelter packed with extra shielding gives the most. The exact levels for the greenhouse, rover and habitat are made up for the game.

source.title: Spacesuits, NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-050
source.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer

facts.kid: Some plants in Moon soil turned dark reddish instead of green. Plant scientists see this color change as a sign that a plant is stressed, a bit like a warning light.

source.title: Plants grown in Apollo lunar regolith present stress-associated transcriptomes that inform prospects for lunar exploration (Paul, Elardo & Ferl)

facts.kid: Moon soil that has sat on the surface longer, hit by space particles and tiny meteorites, is called 'mature'. The Apollo 11 soil was the most mature, and plants in it struggled the most. Plants in the younger Apollo 17 soil did best.

source.title: Plants grown in Apollo lunar regolith present stress-associated transcriptomes that inform prospects for lunar exploration (Paul, Elardo & Ferl)

facts.kid: Every plant sprouted in Moon soil. But after about a week, the Moon-soil plants grew more slowly and had shorter roots and smaller leaves than plants in the fake Moon soil. Some stayed tiny.

source.title: Plants grown in Apollo lunar regolith present stress-associated transcriptomes that inform prospects for lunar exploration (Paul, Elardo & Ferl)

facts.kid: By checking which genes were switched on, scientists saw the Moon-soil plants acting like plants in salty soil or soil with too many metals. They also showed signs of oxidative stress, a kind of chemical damage inside cells.

source.title: Plants grown in Apollo lunar regolith present stress-associated transcriptomes that inform prospects for lunar exploration (Paul, Elardo & Ferl)

facts.kid: In 2022, scientists planted a small weed called thale cress in real Moon soil brought back by Apollo 11, 12 and 17 astronauts. They also grew it in fake Moon soil made on Earth. After 20 days they studied the plants' genes to see how stressed they were.

source.title: Plants grown in Apollo lunar regolith present stress-associated transcriptomes that inform prospects for lunar exploration (Paul, Elardo & Ferl)

facts.kid: Anthocyanins are natural red, purple and blue colors in plants, like the ones in red cabbage and blueberries. When plants face stress like cold, drought or salty soil, they often make more of them. These pigments help protect plant cells from damage.

source.title: The ncRNAs Involved in the Regulation of Abiotic Stress-Induced Anthocyanin Biosynthesis in Plants

facts.kid: When the Sun is shining, solar panels power the base and also charge up energy storage, like batteries. When it gets dark, the base uses that stored energy. Lunar nights can be very long and cold, so NASA is also testing special batteries and fuel cells that can store lots of energy.

source.title: Energy Storage for Lunar Surface Exploration (Guzik et al.)

facts.kid: Making electricity is only half the job. Cables, switches, and converters carry the power to the places that need it, like habitats, rovers, and science tools. NASA is designing a lunar power network that can grow bigger as the Moon Base grows.

source.title: Moon Base Systems

facts.kid: When there is not enough power, the crew and Mission Control turn off less important equipment so the batteries do not run too low. The most important systems stay on. This is called load shedding, and the space station really does it.

source.title: ISS solar array positioning and powerdowns (IAF 2015 draft paper)

facts.kid: In the game you check a power dashboard yourself. On the real space station, a team in Mission Control on Earth watches the station's power all day and night. One console, called SPARTAN, runs the solar arrays and power system and plans how to save power when needed.

source.title: Mission Control: Station in Motion (Houston We Have a Podcast, Ep. 369)

facts.kid: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. Near the Moon's South Pole the Sun stays low in the sky, so NASA is testing tall solar panels that stand straight up, about 10 meters (32 feet) high, to catch the sunlight. They can fold down and be moved to a new spot.

source.title: Three Companies to Help NASA Advance Solar Array Technology for Moon

facts.kid: Galactic cosmic rays are super-fast bits of atoms that come from far beyond our Solar System, from elsewhere in our Milky Way galaxy. They rain down all the time, from every direction, like a steady drizzle. They are so energetic that normal spacecraft walls stop very few of them. When the Sun is very active, slightly fewer reach us.

source.title: Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection, NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020 (Rev G)
source.publisher: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer

facts.kid: Sometimes the Sun has a huge eruption that shoots out a storm of very fast protons. The fastest can cross from the Sun to Earth in minutes. A storm can last hours or days. The particles swirl along the Sun’s magnetic field, so during a storm they can come from almost every direction.

source.title: Solar Radiation Storm

facts.kid: Moon dust is very fine, sharp and often glassy, because there is no wind or water to smooth it. Breathing it may hurt the lungs, and it may scratch skin and eyes. Its surfaces are chemically active and contain tiny bits of iron. One Apollo astronaut got 'lunar hay fever' from it.

source.title: Risk of Adverse Health Effects from Lunar Dust Exposure (James & Kahn-Mayberry), Human Health and Performance Risks of Space Exploration Missions, Ch. 13
source.publisher: NASA Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center

facts.kid: Earth soil is full of rotted leaves, tiny living things and nutrients. Moon 'soil' is crushed rock and glass made by billions of years of space rocks hitting the Moon. It has no organic matter, so plants grown in it need added nutrients.

source.title: Leveraging Lunar Regolith to Further Space Exploration

facts.kid: Moon dust is almost half oxygen, but the oxygen is locked inside minerals. One way to free it is to heat the dust with carbon to about 1,800 degrees Celsius. NASA has tested this on Earth with fake Moon dust, and the oxygen could one day be used for breathing or rocket propellant.

source.title: Environmental Testing of a Fully Automated Carbothermal Reactor for Lunar Oxygen Production
source.publisher: NASA Technical Reports Server (Johnson Space Center)

facts.kid: Moon dirt, called regolith, makes a free shield. Even a thin layer over a shelter blocks most of a solar storm. Cosmic rays are much harder: piling on more dirt helps only a little unless the layer is very thick, like burying the base under meters of soil.

source.title: How NASA Will Protect Astronauts From Space Radiation at the Moon

facts.kid: NASA built a rover called VIPER to hunt for Moon ice. While it drives, a neutron sensor looks for hydrogen hiding underground, a clue that ice may be there. At a good spot, its TRIDENT drill digs up soil from about 1 meter down so other tools can check it. VIPER has not landed on the Moon yet.

source.title: VIPER Rover and Instruments

facts.kid: More stuff between you and the radiation usually means fewer particles reach you, like hiding behind a thicker wall in a snowball fight. This works very well for solar storms. Cosmic rays are trickier: they smash material into smaller particles, so a bit of extra wall barely helps unless the shield is really thick.

source.title: How NASA Will Protect Astronauts From Space Radiation at the Moon

facts.kid: Solar flares are sorted by strength into classes A, B, C, M and X. A is the weakest and X is the strongest. Each class is 10 times stronger than the one before, so an X flare is 100 times stronger than a C flare. A number adds detail: C1.8 is a small C flare.

source.title: Solar Storms and Flares

facts.kid: A solar flare is a giant flash of energy on the Sun. A coronal mass ejection (CME) is a huge cloud of solar material blasted into space. A fast CME pushes a shock wave, like a speedboat’s wave, that speeds up protons and other charged atoms. Parker Solar Probe flies close to the Sun to study this.

source.title: To Protect Artemis II Astronauts, NASA Experts Keep Eyes on Sun

facts.kid: Space radiation is made of tiny, super-fast particles you cannot see or feel. Outside Earth’s magnetic bubble, astronauts get hit by many more of them. NASA says it is one of the biggest health dangers for astronauts, because over time it can raise the risk of cancer and other illnesses.

source.title: Space Radiation (Human Research Program hazard page)

facts.kid: Scientists on Earth watch the Sun day and night. If a solar storm starts, sensors and alarms warn the crew. Anyone outside heads back inside quickly, and if radiation keeps rising, the crew moves into the best-shielded spot until it is safe again.

source.title: To Protect Artemis II Astronauts, NASA Experts Keep Eyes on Sun

facts.kid: Astronauts cannot bring heavy extra walls, so they reuse what they already carry. In Orion, during a solar storm, the crew piles bags of food, water and supplies around themselves to build a shelter. In a Moon base, water tanks and stored supplies can do the same job.

source.title: Scientists and Engineers Evaluate Orion Radiation Protection Plan

facts.kid: Moon ice is mixed into dusty soil. If you heat the soil, the ice turns into water vapor, a gas. The vapor flows through pipes to a very cold surface called a cold trap, where it freezes into frost, like your breath fogging a cold window. Then the ice can be melted and stored.

source.title: Microwave Extraction of Water from Lunar Regolith Simulant
source.publisher: NASA Technical Reports Server (Marshall Space Flight Center)

facts.kid: Materials full of hydrogen, like water and some plastics, stop solar storm particles well for their weight and make fewer extra particles than metals do. For solar storms they beat metals like aluminum. For cosmic rays the benefit is smaller and still being studied.

source.title: Evaluating Shielding Effectiveness for Reducing Space Radiation Cancer Risks (Cucinotta, Kim, Ren)

facts.kid: Moon ice is not clean. It is mixed with dust and other frozen gases like ammonia and carbon dioxide. Before the water is split into oxygen or used by astronauts, it must be cleaned, for example by freezing it carefully to separate the other gases and passing it through very fine filters.

source.title: Technology Assessment for Producing Propellant From Lunar Water
source.publisher: NASA Technical Reports Server (Johnson Space Center)

facts.kid: Space station crews get food deliveries from Earth. Far from Earth, deliveries are rare, and vitamins in packaged food slowly break down. Growing fresh plants can add healthy food and help crews stay longer. For now, grown food is meant to add to packaged food, not replace it.

source.title: Growing Plants in Space
